passage: Ramesh, put your head here on my knee, the oil is warm. I am Yamini, your Dadi. When I was small, we had a mango tree behind the house, and my sister and I would race to be first under it when the wind blew. Once I got there and found a green snake curled up asleep under the fruit! You are giggling. Yes, I screamed too. Now tell me, why did I not run away? You say because I was frozen. Very good guess. You ask me such good questions, beta. I will tell you the rest of the mango story tomorrow, and you must remember where I stopped.

qa.q: What did Dadi's sister and she race to do when the wind blew?
qa.a: They raced to be first under the mango tree.

qa.q: What might Ramesh be feeling as he rests his head on his grandmother's knee?
qa.a: He probably feels warm, safe and curious, since he giggles, guesses answers and asks good questions. 🙂

qa.q: What could Ramesh do to keep these moments meaningful?
qa.a: He can keep listening, ask about the parts he wants to know and remember where the story stopped so it can be picked up tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Ramesh asks her questions?
qa.a: Dadi likely feels happy and valued, since she praises his questions and promises to tell the rest tomorrow.

grounding: A grandmother tells old stories while oiling her grandchild's hair; he listens, asks questions and feels warmth and belonging.

passage: Dada was on the verandah again, tapping his stick. "Always carry a cloth for the sun, Sudha. And never trust the second offer." Sudha had heard it forty times. She rolled her eyes and muttered, "Dada, that was your time, not now." His stick went quiet. The village lane was dusty and the buffalo bell clanked far away. Sudha felt a small pinch in her chest. That evening she sat next to him and said, "I am sorry, Dada. I will take the cloth. Tell me about the second offer." His eyes crinkled. She still planned to choose her own school bag, but she listened.

qa.q: What did Dada tell Sudha to always carry?
qa.a: He told her to always carry a cloth for the sun.

qa.q: What made Sudha feel a small pinch in her chest?
qa.a: She had rolled her eyes and spoken rudely, and when the stick went quiet she realised she had hurt her grandfather.

qa.q: What could Sudha do the next time the advice feels old-fashioned?
qa.a: She can listen patiently, thank him and still make her own choices, without rolling her eyes or answering rudely.

qa.q: How might Dada have felt when Sudha said, "that was your time, not now"?
qa.a: Dada probably felt dismissed and a little hurt, which is why his tapping stopped.

grounding: A child irritated by her grandfather's repeated advice answers rudely, feels the cost, and listens patiently while keeping her own choices.

passage: At the edge of the village, Kunal's Dadi kept a steel tin of laddoos under the bed just for him. "Skip the cow-shed today, beta, sit and eat," she said. Kunal loved it. His younger brother Samir watched, chewing slowly. When Mummy came in from the fields, Kunal swallowed and said, "Dadi gave me sweets, and I will feed the calf now, before dinner." He did not say Dadi had told him to skip it. Samir raised his eyebrows. Later Kunal whispered, "Dadi's love is sweet. Mummy's is a schedule. I need both." Samir laughed and asked for a laddoo.

qa.q: Where did Dadi keep the tin of laddoos?
qa.a: She kept a steel tin of laddoos under the bed.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling as he ate the sweets, and what did he do when Mummy came in?
qa.a: He felt happy and loved by Dadi, yet he still owned up to his chore and said he would feed the calf.

qa.q: What did Kunal do well in balancing Dadi's treats and Mummy's rules?
qa.a: He enjoyed his grandmother's sweets without using her as an excuse against his mother. 😊

qa.q: How might Samir have seen the situation?
qa.a: Samir probably saw his brother getting a treat and wondered whether he would use it as an excuse, and was amused when Kunal did not.

grounding: A child enjoys his grandmother's sweets and skipped chores without using her against his parents' rules.

passage: Saturday night. Today was my birthday. Gopika promised on Monday and again on Thursday that she would come. I put the balloons up myself and kept the good chair for her. She did not come, and no one called. I kept looking at the door while we cut the cake. Everyone else was there, but my chest felt heavy. I am not going to snap at her, and I will not stop talking to her either. On Monday I will say, "I felt sad when you did not come. What happened?" I want to know first. Sangeeta.

qa.q: How many times did Gopika promise she would come?
qa.a: Gopika promised on Monday and again on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling as she kept looking at the door?
qa.a: She felt hurt and disappointed, and her chest felt heavy even with everyone else at the party.

qa.q: What is Sangeeta's plan for talking with Gopika, and why might it work?
qa.a: She plans to say calmly how she felt and ask what happened. Speaking without snapping gives Gopika a chance to explain and keeps the friendship open. 🙂

qa.q: How might Gopika see Monday's conversation if she had a good reason for missing the party?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Sangeeta asked rather than accused, and want to explain and apologise.

grounding: A child hurt that her friend missed her birthday plans to tell her calmly what it felt like and ask why.

passage: Imran came to Usha's veranda at dusk with mud on his shoes. "I am sorry," he said. "I promised to help you with the goat pen, but my father needed me at the well, and I could not send word." Usha crossed her arms. She had waited by the pen all afternoon. But his voice was steady and he looked at her when he spoke. "All right. I forgive you. Next time, ask someone to tell me." She noticed that she would not lend him her best pencil this week. "But if you forget again, I will tell you straight." Imran nodded and picked up the bucket.

qa.q: Why could Imran not help Usha with the goat pen?
qa.a: His father needed him at the well and he could not send word.

qa.q: What might Usha still be worried about after forgiving Imran?
qa.a: She may worry it could happen again, so she stays careful for a while, as when she would not lend him her best pencil that week.

qa.q: What worked in how Usha handled the broken promise?
qa.a: She forgave him and told him what to do next time, and said she would tell him plainly if he forgot again.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Usha crossed her arms?
qa.a: Imran probably felt nervous and guilty, and he showed it by apologising directly and looking at her.

grounding: A child forgives a friend who apologises and explains, stays a little careful, and says she will speak up if it keeps happening.

passage: In the school yard in Accra, Kofi walked around the long way so he would not pass Dalia's class. Last Friday he had promised to help her paint the set for the play, but he went to play football instead and never said a word. Now his ears burned whenever he saw her. All week he hid behind the water tank at lunch. On Thursday he saw her holding a heavy board alone, and his stomach turned. He walked across the yard and said, "I did not come because I chose football. I am sorry. Can I paint with you now?" Dalia looked at him for a moment and handed him a brush.

qa.q: Which city is the school in?
qa.a: The school is in Accra.

qa.q: Why did Kofi avoid Dalia's class and hide behind the water tank?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and ashamed for breaking his promise to help paint the set.

qa.q: What did Kofi do that started to repair things?
qa.a: He told her the truth, said sorry and offered to paint with her, instead of hiding any longer.

qa.q: How might Dalia have felt when Kofi finally came over?
qa.a: Dalia may have felt let down earlier and cautious, but she seemed willing to accept the honest apology, since she handed him a brush.

grounding: A child ashamed of breaking his promise hides for a week, then tells his friend the truth, apologises and offers to make it up.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 5. I have watched Ankita and Jyoti for several weeks. Jyoti often promises to bring the shared chart paper or to save a seat, then forgets. On Tuesday Ankita heard Jyoti promise again and just said, "Okay," without her usual smile. She then brought her own paper. She still chatted with Jyoti at recess and shared her tiffin, but she no longer waited for her at the gate. I spoke to Ankita privately. She said, "I like her, but I won't trust her with the important stuff." I told her that was a fair choice. I will also talk gently with Jyoti about follow-through.

qa.q: What does Jyoti often promise to bring or do?
qa.a: Jyoti often promises to bring the shared chart paper or to save a seat.

qa.q: What does Ankita's plain "Okay" without her usual smile suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she has stopped believing Jyoti's promises after being let down, though she is still polite.

qa.q: What could Ankita keep doing so she stays careful without being cruel?
qa.a: She can stay friendly at recess and share her tiffin but arrange her own supplies for important things instead of relying on Jyoti.

qa.q: How might Jyoti experience the change in Ankita?
qa.a: Jyoti may notice Ankita is less warm and does not wait at the gate, and could feel hurt or confused until someone helps her see why.

grounding: A teacher's note on a child who, after repeated broken promises, stops relying on her friend for big things but stays friendly.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage:
"Mummy, Ma'am said I broke Vihaan's compass, but I never touched it."
"Sit down, Ojas. Take a breath. What happened?"
"My face went hot. I shouted, and she said I was being rude."
"Did you see who did?"
"It was on the front bench. I was in the library the whole period, and Ruchi saw me."
"Then tomorrow we will talk to your teacher together, calmly, with those facts."
"Will she believe me?"
"I do not know. But she should give you a fair hearing."
"Okay. I will not shout this time."
Trisha squeezed his hand.

qa.q: Where was Ojas during the period the compass broke?
qa.a: He was in the library the whole period.

qa.q: Why did Ojas's face go hot?
qa.a: He felt the unfairness of being blamed for something he had not done, and it made him shout.

qa.q: What could Ojas do tomorrow to get a fair hearing?
qa.a: He can explain calmly with facts, such as that he was in the library and Ruchi saw him, and let his mother come along.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen the shouting?
qa.a: The teacher may have seen it as rudeness and taken it as a sign of guilt, so staying calm and giving facts could change her view.

grounding: A child blamed by his teacher for something he did not do tells his mother, and plans to explain calmly with facts and a fair hearing.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage: After lunch break in the Class 6 corridor, the vase lay in pieces and Mrs. Iyer was asking who did it. Nitin saw Hafsa look at the floor. "It was Nitin," said someone, and Hafsa said nothing. Nitin took the blame, and his eyes stung. That evening, in the school van, he said, "Hafsa, I saw you knock it." She flushed and whispered, "I was scared of my father." Nitin looked out of the window for a while. "I was hurt," he said. "I want to hear more, but I do not know yet if we are friends the same way."

qa.q: What lay in pieces in the corridor?
qa.a: The vase lay in pieces.

qa.q: Why did Nitin's eyes sting when he took the blame?
qa.a: He felt betrayed, because he had seen Hafsa knock the vase and she let him carry the blame.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that avoided revenge and left room for repair?
qa.a: He told Hafsa what he had seen, listened to her reason and said he needed time to decide about the friendship.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt in the van when Nitin spoke?
qa.a: Hafsa probably felt ashamed and afraid, and she may have wanted to explain why she stayed silent.

grounding: A child takes blame that a friend let fall on him; he tells her what he saw, hears her out and decides slowly about repairing trust.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage: Mridul, you look tense. Let me tell you what I did at ten. I am Eshaan, your Mama. A window in our school broke during cricket, and it was my shot. When the headmaster asked, my friend Bhaskar was standing next to me, and I said nothing. He got a week of lunches in the office. I felt sick every night; I could not enjoy my dal. On Monday my knees shook, but I walked to my teacher and told her it was me. Then I found Bhaskar and said sorry. He was angry for a few days. The fear passed in an hour, and the regret would have stayed with me.

qa.q: Whose shot broke the window?
qa.a: It was Eshaan's shot.

qa.q: Why could Eshaan not enjoy his dal?
qa.a: He felt sick and guilty for letting Bhaskar take the blame.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do that fixed part of the problem?
qa.a: He went to his teacher, told her the truth, and then apologised to Bhaskar.

qa.q: How might Bhaskar have felt when Eshaan first said nothing?
qa.a: Bhaskar probably felt let down and unfairly punished, and that is likely why he stayed angry for a few days.

grounding: An elder recalls letting a friend take the blame out of fear, feeling sick, then admitting the truth to the teacher and apologising.
